column5: YHWH king over all earth “on that day”
column6: The commentary's day transfers undivided rule to its Mālik; Zechariah says YHWH will be king over all the earth and, on that day, one with one name. It makes royal exclusivity explicitly eschatological.

column5: court sits and a ruler's dominion is removed
column6: Daniel's court sits and strips the hostile ruler of dominion for destruction. It supplies a concrete court-scene counterpart to the commentary's claim that human possession and command fail on the day of judgment.

column5: the world's kingdom becomes the Lord's kingdom
column6: At the seventh trumpet the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of God and his Christ, who reigns forever. This gives the commentary's exclusive final sovereignty an apocalyptic Christian formulation.

column5: Abel's blood cries from the ground
column6: The commentary fears blood going lost when it is not avenged; Abel's blood cries from the ground to God, making shed blood an enduring claimant rather than a forgotten event.

column5: the earth reveals blood and no longer covers its slain
column6: In Isaiah's judgment setting, the earth discloses its bloodshed and stops concealing those killed. It joins the commentary's resurrection setting to its image of blood that cannot vanish without answer.

column5: blood given to blood-shedders as their due
column6: Because the persecutors poured out the blood of saints and prophets, the bowl judgment gives them blood to drink, “for they deserve it.” This makes bloodshed itself the measure of eschatological recompense.

column5: false balance versus a full weight
column6: A false balance is an abomination while a full weight delights YHWH. The proverb directly supplies the commentary's contrast between a tipped scale and its exact, acceptable counterweight.

column5: just balances, ephah, and bath
column6: Ezekiel's restored commonwealth is ordered to use just balances and standard measures. It gives the commentary's upright scale a public, ruler-governed economic setting.

column5: full, pressed, shaken, overflowing measure returned
column6: Jesus promises a good measure, pressed down and shaken together, returned into the giver's lap, and adds that the measure used returns to its user. This turns the commentary's full measure into a precise reciprocity formula.

column5: by the measure one measures, so one is measured
column6: The Mishnah states its measure-for-measure principle while interpreting the sotah ordeal. It gives later Jewish formulation to the commentary's balance as equivalent retribution rather than mere market accuracy.

column5: stand in allotted place at the end of days
column6: Daniel is told to rest and then stand in his allotted place at the end of days. This is an unusually direct pairing of resurrection-like standing and the final temporal horizon developed in the commentary.

column5: all in tombs hear the judge's voice
column6: Jesus says that all who are in tombs will hear his voice. It supplies the universal summons that precedes the two resurrection outcomes in the following verse and the commentary's standing scene.

column5: sea, Death, and Hades return their dead
column6: The sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead, after which each is judged by deeds. It provides the return-from-every-custodian detail missing from the commentary's compressed resurrection image.

column5: all nations gathered and separated before the throne
column6: All nations are gathered before the enthroned Son of Man and separated as sheep from goats. It supplies the assembled-humanity action between the royal throne and the divergent final rewards.

column5: YHWH comes to judge earth in righteousness
column6: The psalm announces YHWH's coming to judge the world in righteousness and peoples in faithfulness. Its universal, equitable judgment fills out the commentary's claim that the day is a true accounting.

column5: day of YHWH as darkness, not light
column6: Those who desire YHWH's day are warned that it is darkness rather than light. This gives the commentary's severe event-day a prophetic reversal of complacent expectation.

column5: day of the Lord arrives like a thief
column6: Paul says the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. It makes the commentary's day an arriving event that overtakes people rather than an abstract date.

column5: sudden destruction with no escape
column6: The claim of peace and safety is followed by sudden destruction that cannot be escaped. This gives the prior day-of-the-Lord image its inescapable consequence.

column5: day comes; created order passes and works are exposed
column6: The day of the Lord arrives like a thief, the heavens and elements pass away, and the earth's works are exposed. It enlarges the commentary's day-as-event into a cosmic disclosure of deeds.

column5: YHWH enters judgment with all flesh
column6: Isaiah says YHWH enters into judgment with all flesh by fire and sword. It directly combines the commentary's universal judgment, wrath, and punitive outcome.

column5: every transgression receives just retribution
column6: Hebrews says every transgression and disobedience received a just retribution. It states the commentary's dīn as measured return in juridical rather than commercial language.

column5: account to the judge of living and dead
column6: Those opposed to believers will give an account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead. It provides the commentary's account, universal judge, and resurrection horizon in one formula.

column5: kings see the enthroned judge and righteous judgment
column6: The kings, mighty, and landowners see the glorious enthroned figure and recognize that righteous judgment proceeds before him. It gives the commentary's ruler-and-day scene a Second Temple reversal of earthly power.

column5: silver and gold cannot deliver on the day of wrath
column6: Zephaniah says neither silver nor gold can deliver on YHWH's day of wrath. It is a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's claim that a final substitute payment is not accepted.

column5: silver and gold cannot satisfy or deliver in wrath
column6: Ezekiel has people cast away silver and gold because it cannot deliver them on the day of YHWH's wrath. The image explicitly turns valuable payment into useless weight at judgment.

column5: riches do not profit on the day of wrath
column6: The proverb denies that riches profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death. It sharply qualifies the commentary's debt-and-value imagery at the final account.

column5: repay, double, and measure back in the cup
column6: The heavenly command says to repay Babylon as she repaid, double her works, and mix double in her own cup. It gives the commentary's equivalent return and unbending measure an apocalyptic form.

column5: wrongdoer repaid without partiality
column6: The wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong done, with no partiality. This supplies a concise Christian statement of impartial retribution that matches the commentary's exact-scale logic.

column5: a holy way where the unclean do not pass or go astray
column6: Isaiah's eschatological highway is called the holy way; the unclean do not pass on it and even fools do not go astray. It is a close path-and-non-straying counterpart to the commentary's straight path and its contrary ending.

column5: “a ransom has been found” for one going to the pit
column6: Job's heavenly mediator says a ransom has been found and the sufferer should be spared descent to the pit. Its rescue-payment image contrasts with the commentary's final-day refusal of ransom and marks the contextual limit of that refusal.

column5: wicked borrows and does not repay
column6: The psalm contrasts the wicked borrower who does not repay with the righteous giver. It supplies the commentary's ordinary debt-and-payment image in a moral distinction, though not a final court scene.

column5: borrower servant to lender
column6: The proverb says the borrower becomes servant to the lender. It gives the commentary's loan relation a concrete hierarchy of power that complicates its image of sovereign ownership.

column5: withheld wages cry out to the Lord of hosts
column6: The unpaid wages of laborers cry out and their cries reach the Lord of hosts. It transfers the commentary's honest trade and unresolved claim into a social injustice heard by divine authority.

column5: debtor's bill and amount owed to the master
column6: A steward asks a debtor how much is owed to his master and works from the written bill. This gives the debtors and documents that make the preceding command to render an account concrete.

column5: denarius pricing of grain under the balance
column6: The apocalyptic voice fixes grain at a denarius price while preserving oil and wine. It supplies the price-and-coin detail that explains the economic force of the balance in the preceding verse.

column5: level path of the righteous made level by the Upright One
column6: Isaiah calls the righteous person's path level and addresses God as the Upright One who makes it level. It complements the commentary's straight-path image, though it does not itself use a scale.

column5: constricted way leading to life
column6: Jesus contrasts the constricted way leading to life with the broad way to destruction. It gives the commentary's straight path and loss a specific New Testament path-outcome contrast.

column5: postmortem tribunal, records, and Dokiel's balance
column6: In Recension A, souls pass a postmortem tribunal in which deeds are recorded and the archangel Dokiel weighs them. The vision gathers the commentary's standing, accounting, and scale images; chapter divisions vary by edition.

column5: Abel's blood expanded to future righteous descendants
column6: This Palestinian Targum expands Abel's crying blood to include the blood of righteous descendants yet to arise. It intensifies the commentary's claim that blood does not disappear, though wording varies among Targum witnesses.
